title: March notation
summary: A **March test** sweeps through the memory, address by address, with a fixed list of reads and writes. This topic teaches the notation used to write March tests, shows how one element runs, and how to compute the length of a test.
objectives: Explain what a March test is and why it suits memory BIST.
Read March notation: elements, address orders ⇑ ⇓ ⇕ and operations r0, r1, w0, w1.
Run a March element by hand on a small memory.
Compute the length of a March test (kN) and its test time.

subsections.title: From fault models to an algorithm

blocks.md:
In *Memories and Their Faults* every fault model asked for certain operations: read both values, make both transitions, operate on an aggressor and then read the victim, sweep the addresses **up and down**. A good memory test must do all of this for **every** cell — and still be short.

The answer, found in the late 1970s and 1980s, is the **March test**: the test *marches* through the memory, one address after the other, and at every address applies the same short list of operations. Then it marches again, maybe in the other direction, with a different list.

blocks.title: Why March tests rule memory BIST
blocks.md:
- **Linear length**: the number of operations grows as k·N for N addresses — fast even for big memories.
- **Provable**: for each fault model you can show *on paper* that the test detects it.
- **Cheap in hardware**: an address counter that counts up or down, a data generator for 0/1, and a comparator — exactly the MBIST hardware of the later trainings.

steps.title: A list of elements
steps.md: A March test is written in braces { } as a list of **March elements** separated by semicolons. The elements run one after the other.

steps.title: One element
steps.md: Each element is an **address order** followed by a list of **operations** in brackets.

steps.title: Address order
steps.md: **⇑** goes up through all addresses, **⇓** goes down, **⇕** means the order does not matter (either is fine).

steps.title: Operations
steps.md: **r0 / r1** read and expect 0 / 1; **w0 / w1** write 0 / 1. At every address, all operations of the element are done before the next address.

steps.title: Length
steps.md: Count the operations: 1 + 2 + 2 = **5 per address**. For N addresses the test needs **5N** operations.

rows: address order down: N−1, … 1, 0 — exactly the reverse of ⇑
any order — the test works with either
read the cell, compare with 0 / 1 — a mismatch is a **fail**
general form: x is 0 or 1, x̄ is its inverse
a pause with no access — used for retention tests (Topic 5)
blocks.caption: March notation

blocks.title: ⇑ does not have to be 0, 1, 2 …
blocks.md: Any fixed sequence that visits every address once can be '⇑' — for example a counter that counts in Gray code. The only rule: **⇓ must be exactly the reverse of ⇑**. MBIST hardware uses this freedom to save logic.

steps.title: Start
steps.md: The previous element ⇕(w0) has written 0 into every cell. Now ⇑(r0, w1) starts at address 0.

steps.title: Address 0
steps.md: Read: expect 0 — it is 0 ✓. Write 1. Only now the test moves on.

steps.title: Address 1
steps.md: The same two operations at address 1.

steps.title: Address 2
steps.md: And at address 2. Note that address 0 and 1 already hold 1 — they can act as **aggressors** for cells that are not visited yet.

steps.title: Address 3
steps.md: After the last address the element is finished: **2 operations × 4 addresses = 8 operations**, and every cell holds 1 for the next element.

blocks.title: The operations of one address come back to back
blocks.md: In ⇑(r0, w1) the read and the write of one address follow each other directly; the next address only comes afterwards. This order matters: it decides which cells are still 0 and which already 1 when a cell is read — and that is how coupling faults are caught.

blocks.prompt: Practice: put the operations of the element ⇓(r1, w0) on a 3-address memory in the order they happen.

blocks.md:
The **length** of a March test is the number of operations per address, k, written as **kN**. With one operation per clock, the test time is

> test time = k · N · clock period

Memories in a chip are tested at their functional clock, often several hundred MHz.

columns: Time for 1 Mi words at 100 MHz
blocks.caption: Linear tests stay short; a test that grows with N² is useless for big memories

blocks.title: Count the operations, not the elements
blocks.md: {⇕(w0); ⇑(r0, w1); ⇑(r1, w0); ⇓(r0, w1); ⇓(r1, w0); ⇕(r0)} has 6 elements but 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 = **10** operations per address → **10N**.

questions.text: What is the length of {⇕(w0); ⇑(r0, w1); ⇑(r1, w0); ⇕(r0)}?
What does ⇓ mean in a March element?
options: Visit the addresses in the reverse of the ⇑ order.
The order of addresses does not matter.

questions.text: In the element ⇑(r0, w1), what happens at one address before the test moves to the next address?
options: The cell is read (expecting 0) and then 1 is written into it.
Only the read; all writes come after all reads.
The cell is written with 0 and then read.

questions.text: The element ⇑(r1, w0) runs on a 2-address memory. Put the operations in order.

options: Their length grows only linearly with the number of addresses.
Their fault coverage can be proven for each fault model.
